content.text: Biritch, or Russian Whist, is the earliest known form of Bridge â€” the game that the word 'Bridge' originally referred to before Auction Bridge and Contract Bridge evolved from it. It is a 4-player partnership trick-taking game using a standard 52-card deck. Unlike Whist, no trump is turned up; instead the dealer (or dealer's partner) declares trumps or calls 'biritch' (no-trump). The dealer's partner's hand is then exposed as a 'Dummy', played by the dealer â€” the defining innovation that would eventually lead to modern Contract Bridge.

The game was played in the Russian colony at Constantinople (Istanbul) during the 1880s. John Collinson, a British railway engineer working in Turkey between 1880â€“1884, learned the game there and introduced it to friends in England. He published a small booklet titled 'Biritch, or Russian Whist' on 9 July 1886, registered at Stationers' Hall â€” the earliest known document describing any form of Bridge.
4 players in fixed partnerships, seated opposite each other. Cutting for partners, shuffling, and dealing are the same as at Short Whist.
Standard 52-card deck. Card ranking as at Whist: A (high), K, Q, J, 10, 9, 8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2.
13 cards dealt to each player. Unlike Whist, NO card is turned up for trumps.

items.text: Auction Bridge (Successor): Evolved from Biritch in the 1900s. All four players bid competitively for the right to name trumps, replacing fixed dealer declaration.
Contract Bridge (Modern Successor): Developed by Harold Vanderbilt in 1925. Only tricks bid and won count toward game; overtricks score separately. The dominant form of Bridge today.
